title: The Art of Staying Ahead of Deadlines Improved Algorithms for the Minimum Tardy Processing Time

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The lemma reads \sum_{i\in[n]} |\tilde S_j \setminus S_{j-1}| \le d_max+1 and the proof writes |{i \in [n] \mid x \in \tilde S_j \setminus S_{j-1}}| \le 1: the summation/counting index is i, but the summand depends on j, which is free. The analogous Lemma 4.1 correctly uses j throughout. As written, the sum is just n times a fixed term and the proof's counting step is meaningless.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 'Leveraging Dynamic Strings' ('We represent a set S ⊆ [n] ...')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says 'We represent a set S ⊆ [n] by its corresponding indicator string x_S ∈ {0,1}^u, i.e., i ∈ S iff x_S[i]=1.' The sets being encoded are sets of attainable processing times, i.e. subsets of [0..d_max] = [0..u-1], not subsets of the job index set [n]. With u = d_max+1 there is no reason for the universe to be [n], and the indicator-string definition is inconsistent with the rest of the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 'Leveraging Dynamic Strings' (trim step split(0^{p_j} x_{L_{j-1}}, u))
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: x_{L_{j-1}} is the prefix of x_{S_{j-1}} up to position d_j - p_j, so it has length d_j - p_j + 1; after prepending 0^{p_j} the string has length d_j + 1 ≤ d_max + 1 = u. Hence the string is never longer than u and the claimed 'trim to length u' is vacuous; worse, split requires the index to lie in [0..|x|), and u ≥ |x| = d_j+1, so the call split(·, u) is ill-defined. What is actually needed is right-padding with zeros to length u so that the subsequent bitwise OR with x_{S_{j-1}} operates on equal-length strings.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 'Our Approach' / 'Leveraging Dynamic Strings' (split at position d_j - p_j)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The algorithm always splits x_{S_{j-1}} at position d_j - p_j and splits 0^u at position p_j, but no case distinction is made for jobs with p_j > d_j (and hence d_j - p_j < 0), which are always tardy. For such jobs the split index is negative (resp. p_j may exceed u-1), violating the precondition i ∈ [0..|x|) of the split operation in Lemma 3.1.

The text says 'we first split S_j into two parts w.r.t. d_j - p_j, i.e., we obtain L_{j-1} := S_{j-1} ∩ [0..d_j - p_j] and R_{j-1} := S_{j-1} ∩ (d_j - p_j..d_j]'. The set being split is S_{j-1}, not S_j (S_j is not yet computed at that point); the sentence contradicts the displayed definitions.

The feasibility condition is stated as '∑_{i∈J*: i≤j} p_i ≤ d_j for all j ∈ J'. The constraint must be required only for the selected (early) jobs, i.e. for all j ∈ J*; requiring it for all jobs j in the whole instance is a different (stronger, incorrect) condition, and 'J' is never defined.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4 (multi-machine), Lemma 4.1 and the claimed Õ(n + d_max^m) bound
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Lemma 4.1 only bounds the total number of element insertions by (d_max+1)^m; it does not bound the number of dynamic-string operations per job. Trimming 'point-wise, for each of the m (independent) entries' of an m-dimensional array flattened into a single string generally requires Ω(d_max^{m-1}) split/concat operations per job (one per block along the faster-varying dimensions), which would give Õ(n·d_max^{m-1} + d_max^m) rather than the claimed Õ(n + d_max^m). No implementation details are given to justify the stated bound.

predicted_errors.error_location: End of Section 4 ('the adapted multi-dimensional dynamic string data structure, remains the same as in Fischer and Wennmann [5]')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Fischer and Wennmann's work addresses the single-machine problem 1||∑p_jU_j; attributing an 'adapted multi-dimensional dynamic string data structure' for the m-machine setting to that reference appears to misrepresent its content, and no pointer to such a construction is given.

With the paper's 0-based string indexing, a string x has positions 0..|x|-1, so the output 'x(i..|x|]' refers to position |x|, which does not exist; the second piece should be x(i..|x|) (positions i+1..|x|-1). The stated operation is inconsistent with the stated index convention.
